# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

### Introduction
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has revolutionized the treatment of severe aortic stenosis across all surgical risk spectrums [1]. While transfemoral (TF) retrograde delivery is the gold-standard approach, approximately 5% to 15% of patients are deemed ineligible due to hostile anatomy, severe peripheral arterial disease (PAD), or significant vessel tortuosity [1,2]. Early alternative strategies, such as surgical transapical or transaortic access, are associated with increased morbidity and longer hospital stays [1,2]. This has driven the clinical development of percutaneous, extrathoracic approaches [2]. Among these, transcaval (caval-aortic) access has emerged as a robust fully percutaneous strategy [2]. Following pre-clinical validation [3], the first-in-human transcaval TAVR was successfully performed in 2014 [4], establishing a pathway directly from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the adjacent infrarenal abdominal aorta.

### Pre-Procedural Planning and Procedural Technique
Meticulous pre-procedural planning is mandatory and relies primarily on contrast-enhanced multidetector computed tomography (CT) [5]. CT imaging is used to identify a calcium-free crossing target on the anterior or right-lateral wall of the abdominal aorta that lies in close proximity to the IVC, without any interposed structures such as loops of bowel [5,6]. The suitability of patient anatomy is thoroughly quantified on CT prior to intervention [6]. 

The procedure itself is performed under fluoroscopic guidance [7]. An electrified 0.014-inch guidewire is used to cross the retroperitoneal space from the IVC to the aorta, where it is captured by a snare pre-positioned in the aorta [7,8]. Once the tract is established, a large-bore sheath is introduced [7]. Despite creating a temporary aortocaval connection, the relative safety of the procedure is underpinned by retroperitoneal hydrostatic pressure exceeding central venous pressure, causing any aortic bleeding around the sheath to decompress harmlessly into the lower-pressure IVC [3,4].

### Clinical Evidence and Outcomes in TAVR
The primary clinical validation of transcaval TAVR was established in a prospective, multicenter clinical trial of 100 patients ineligible for TF access, which reported a 99% access success rate and 98% successful port closure with nitinol cardiac occluders [9]. Long-term follow-up at 12 months demonstrated safe tract healing, high rates of fistula closure, and excellent survival with no late vascular complications [10]. Real-world applicability was further demonstrated in a multicenter European registry [11]. Over time, these experiences have been consolidated into standardized best practices and procedural recommendations to optimize safety [12].

When compared directly with other access methods, single-center and multicenter studies have confirmed the utility of the transcaval approach [13]. For instance, a propensity-weighted analysis using the Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology (STS/ACC) TVT Registry compared transcaval to transaxillary access, showing that the transcaval approach was associated with a five-fold lower rate of stroke and transient ischemic attacks, and higher rates of direct discharge to home [14]. Extensive meta-analyses [15] and comparative cohort studies [16] have confirmed that transcaval access offers a safe and highly viable option when TF access is contraindicated, displaying comparable clinical outcomes and mortality rates to other extrathoracic alternative routes.

### Technical Refinements and Case Variations
Technical refinements have further expanded the feasibility of the transcaval approach. While earlier cohorts required general anesthesia, contemporary series describe minimalistic transcaval TAVR under conscious sedation, which significantly reduces procedural time and length of hospital stay [17]. The transcaval route has also facilitated the deployment of novel self-expanding devices for pure aortic regurgitation [18]. Meticulous planning has even permitted safe transcaval access directly through pre-existing abdominal aortic endografts or polyester grafts [19,20]. Furthermore, the introduction of secondary radial artery access for cerebral protection and procedural monitoring minimizes femoral arterial complications associated with secondary access sites [21].

### Broader Non-TAVR Applications
Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has found extensive applications in other large-bore vascular and structural interventions. It has successfully enabled thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) in patients with severe iliac disease [22,23]. In vascular surgery, transcaval access is utilized as an elegant method for the embolization of persistent type II endoleaks following endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) [24,25]. A systematic review of transcaval endoleak embolizations has highlighted technical success rates exceeding 95% with low post-procedural morbidity [26].

In the field of temporary mechanical circulatory support (MCS), transcaval access facilitates the rapid, percutaneous delivery of high-flow microaxial pumps, such as the Impella 5.0 or 5.5, in patients with severe cardiogenic shock and hostile peripheral vasculature [27]. By avoiding surgical cutdown, this method provides immediate hemodynamic support and left ventricular unloading [27]. In emergency scenarios, modified transcaval techniques have also enabled left atrial venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) without pre-procedural contrast CT [28].

### Complication Management and Access Closure
Despite its high success, the transcaval approach is associated with potential complications, such as retroperitoneal hemorrhage, aortic dissection, or device embolization [12]. Port closure is conventionally achieved using off-label nitinol cardiac or duct occluders [9]. However, dedicated, purpose-built transcaval closure devices have shown outstanding results in first-in-human studies, achieving immediate, complete closure [29]. Troubleshooting complications, such as managing a persistent pinhole leak or pseudoaneurysm at an abandoned traversal site, emphasizes the necessity of treating the initial puncture site as a strict procedural commitment [30]. Standardized rescue protocols, including the ready availability of covered bailout aortic stents, are essential to ensure procedural safety [12,30].

### Conclusion
Transcaval access represents a major paradigm shift in large-bore interventional cardiology and endovascular surgery. By utilizing electrosurgical techniques and the unique hemodynamics of the caval-aortic tract, it offers a fully percutaneous, safe, and effective alternative to surgical access for high-risk patients. Future refinement of dedicated access and closure devices will likely expand its clinical utility, further improving outcomes in complex structural heart interventions.
